intro: Three rules explain almost every written accent in Spanish.
p.tilde.consejo: The tilde marks the syllable that sounds strongest. It is also called «acento escrito» or «acento ortográfico».
p.sílaba.consejo: «Pa-pel» has two syllables. The syllable that sounds strongest is called the stressed syllable.
p.aguda.glosa: oxytone word (stressed on the last syllable)
p.aguda.consejo: It takes a tilde if it ends in a vowel, n or s: «café», «jamón», «inglés». «Reloj» does not.
p.llana.glosa: paroxytone word (stressed on the second-to-last syllable)
p.llana.consejo: It takes a tilde if it does NOT end in a vowel, n or s: «árbol», «fácil», «lápiz». «Casa» does not. The ll sounds like y.
p.esdrújula.glosa: proparoxytone word (stressed on the third-to-last syllable)
p.esdrújula.consejo: All proparoxytone words take a tilde, with no exception: «médico», «teléfono», «sábado».
p.árbol.consejo: It is paroxytone and ends in l, so it takes a tilde. Its plural, «árboles», takes one too.
p.él.consejo: With a tilde it is the pronoun «he». Without a tilde, «el» is the article: «el libro».
p.sí.consejo: With a tilde it is «yes»; without it, «si» is «if». Compare: «sí, voy» and «si vienes».
p.más.consejo: With a tilde it means «more»: «más café». Without it, «mas» is «but», an old-fashioned word.
p.té.consejo: With a tilde it is the drink. Without it, «te» is a pronoun: «te espero». It rhymes with «bebé».
p.país.consejo: The tilde falls on the í, which sounds strong and separates from the a: «pa-ÍS», two syllables.
p.lápiz.consejo: It is paroxytone and ends in z, so it takes a tilde. In the plural the z becomes c: «lápices».
b1.texto:
Spanish spelling tells you the stress.

1. A word ending in a **vowel, n or s** is stressed on the second-to-last syllable: **ca**sa, **ha**blan, **lu**nes.

2. A word ending in **any other consonant** is stressed on the last syllable: ha**blar**, ciu**dad**, re**loj**.

3. A **tilde** marks every word that breaks rules 1 and 2: ca**fé**, tam**bién**, in**glés**; **ár**bol, **fá**cil, **lá**piz.

4. A word stressed on the third-to-last syllable **always** has a tilde: **mé**dico, te**lé**fono, **dí**melo.

A stressed **i** or **u** next to a, e, o takes a tilde to stand on its own: pa**ís**, d**í**a, r**í**o.

A tilde also separates pairs of short words (see the grammar section) and marks question words, even inside a sentence: no sé **dónde** vive.

Plurals can gain or lose it: joven → **jó**venes; inglés → ingleses; examen → e**xá**menes.
b2.f0.texto: Why does the word café have a tilde?
b2.f1.texto: It is oxytone and ends in a vowel.
b2.f2.texto: What kind of word is árbol?
b2.f3.texto: It is a paroxytone word that ends in a consonant.
b2.f4.texto: It needs a tilde just like lápiz.
b2.f5.texto: The pronoun él always has a tilde.
b2.f6.texto: Without a tilde, the word el is an article.
b2.f7.texto: With a tilde, the word té names a hot drink.
b2.f8.texto: Now I understand the rule for paroxytone words.
b4.titulo: Three kinds of word and tilde pairs
b4.texto:
**Oxytone words** are stressed on the last syllable. They take a tilde if they end in a vowel, n or s: **café, también, inglés**. No tilde: **reloj, ciudad**.

**Paroxytone words** are stressed on the second-to-last. They take a tilde if they do NOT end in a vowel, n or s: **árbol, fácil, lápiz**. No tilde: **casa, lunes**.

**Proparoxytone words** are stressed on the third-to-last. They always take a tilde: **médico, teléfono, sábado**.

**Pairs that the tilde separates**:

- **él** (pronoun) and **el** (article)
- **tú** (pronoun) and **tu** (possessive)
- **mí** (pronoun) and **mi** (possessive)
- **sí** (yes) and **si** (if)
- **sé** (I know) and **se** (pronoun)
- **té** (tea) and **te** (pronoun)
- **más** (more) and **mas** (but, old-fashioned)
- **qué, cuándo, dónde** (questions) and **que, cuando, donde** (connectors)
b4.e0.texto: He has tea with his brother.
b4.e2.texto: Your new pencil is on my table.
b5.f0.texto: In the old classroom it smells of pencil and new paper.
b5.f1.texto: A huge tree spreads its branches over the school yard.
b5.f2.texto: The children carefully draw each tilde over the right vowel.
b5.f3.texto: The morning sun lights up the pages full of words.
b5.f4.texto: On the board, the teacher slowly writes the word país.
b5.f5.texto: A small girl frowns in front of the open notebook.
b5.f6.texto: Her ink-stained fingers hesitate before the last letter.
b5.f7.texto: The teacher comes closer and points out the syllable to her with the pencil.
b5.f8.texto: The golden light comes in through the window and draws a rectangle on the floor.
b5.f9.texto: At last the girl smiles because the tilde now has its place.
b6.o0: Es aguda y acaba en vocal
b6.o0.refuerzo: That is it: it breaks rule 1, so it is marked.
b6.o1.refuerzo: The tilde depends on stress, not on origin.
b6.o2: Todas las palabras en -e la llevan
b6.o2.refuerzo: Most do not: coche, madre, calle.
b7.o0.refuerzo: Without a tilde, «el» is the article: «el hermano».
b7.o1.refuerzo: Well done: the pronoun «he» takes a tilde.
b7.o2.refuerzo: «Le» is an object pronoun, not a subject one.
b7.pregunta: Complete with the pronoun that means «he».
b8.o0.refuerzo: «Casa» is paroxytone and ends in a vowel: it follows rule 1.
b8.o1.refuerzo: «Hablar» is oxytone and ends in r: it follows rule 2.
b8.o2.refuerzo: That is it: paroxytone ending in l, it breaks rule 2.
b9.o0.refuerzo: A question word keeps its tilde inside a sentence.
b9.o1.refuerzo: Without a tilde it is a relative: «la casa donde vive».
b9.pregunta: Complete: I do not know in what place she lives.
b10.frase: Él toma té con su hermano
b10.traduccion: He has tea with his brother
b11.o0.refuerzo: Without a tilde, the stress would move to the second-to-last syllable.
b11.o1.refuerzo: That is it: the tilde keeps the stress on the a.
b11.o2.refuerzo: A noun ending in a consonant adds -es.
p.vocal.consejo: In Spanish the «v» sounds like «b», so «vocal» is pronounced «bo-KAL», stressed on the end.
p.consonante.consejo: Ends in «-nte», so the stress falls on the «NAN», the third syllable.
p.artículo.consejo: It has an accent on the «TI», the stressed syllable, so it is a word with a tilde.
p.nombra.consejo: From «nombre», name. Here the verb means to name or mention something.
p.bebida.consejo: From «beber». The «b» and the «v» sound the same in Spanish, so «bebida» has two «b» sounds.
p.regla.consejo: A word that starts with «r» sounds strong here: «RRE-gla», with a rolled r at the beginning.
p.llanas.consejo: The «ll» sounds like a «y» in most of Spain: «YA-nas», with the stress on the first syllable.
p.justa.consejo: The «j» sounds like an English «h», so «justa» sounds like «HUS-ta».
p.maestra.consejo: The masculine is «maestro». The «-a» ending marks the feminine, so «maestra» is for a woman.
p.frunce.consejo: Before «e» the «c» sounds like «th» in Spain: «FRUN-the», so «fruncir» is pronounced «frun-THIR».
p.manchados.consejo: From «manchar», to stain. Here it describes the fingers and ends in «-dos», plural.
p.dudan.consejo: From «duda», doubt. The «d» at the start is soft, almost like an English «th».
p.ante.consejo: A short word that means «in front of». It is not the same as «antes», which means «before» in time.
p.rectángulo.consejo: Its stress falls on the «TAN». The tilde marks it, and «rec-» comes from «recto», straight.
